extracted.intended_audience: contributors to periodicals, essayists, and literate readers interested in composition, editing, and satire
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing, editing, and presenting short essays and character sketches for a periodical (The Spectator-style), including how to handle submissions, preserve voice, craft satirical portraits, and manage rhetorical tone. Emphasis on manners, moral framing, and editorial ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve contributors' original voice / avoid harmful alteration
rubrics_metrics.description: They might be printed entire, and without any Alteration... there is something so extremely natural and peculiarly good in some of them, that I will appeal to the World whether it was possible to alter a Word in them without doing them a manifest Hurt and Violence; and whether they can ever appear rightly, and, as they ought, but in their own native Dress and Colours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not lightly 'dress' another writer's paper in the editor's own style; avoid cutting or adding material that would damage the piece's natural expression. Publish submissions whole when their native phrasing and manner are integral to their value. If adapting pieces to the 'character and Genius' of your paper, be cautious—only do so when alterations do not 'hurt' the work. Steele's reflection provides examples of initial temptation to repaint contributions and his subsequent judgement that some pieces must remain unaltered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise authorly humility and avoid envy
rubrics_metrics.description: An Author should take all Methods to humble himself in the Opinion he has of his own Performances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and temper feelings of envy toward contributors and other writers; respond with pity or generous judgement rather than concealment or hostile editing. Allow others their share of public applause; humility helps fair editorial decisions about publishing others' work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control passion in depiction and rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: To contain the Spirit of Anger, is the worthiest Discipline we can put our selves to... quick Sensibility is inseparable from a ready Understanding; but why should not that good Understanding call to it self all its Force on such Occasions, to master that sudden Inclination to Anger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In both characterization and authorial tone, avoid unbridled, inconsistent passion. Passion that overrides reason makes characters and rhetoric appear ridiculous or incoherent (illustrated by the quoted mad Alexander). Strive for emotional truth balanced by sober reason so scenes remain credible and persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let argument rely on reason, not loudness or theatrics
rubrics_metrics.description: The Man of Heat replied to every Answer of his Antagonist with a louder Note than ordinary... and to make the greater Impression upon his Hearers, concluded with a loud Thump upon the Table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shouting, rhetorical bluster, or physical theatrics (in scene or in argument) are poor substitutes for clear, forceful reasoning. When depicting disputation, show that true persuasion depends on the quality of argument and elocution rather than on volume or spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of informers and gossip as sources
rubrics_metrics.description: A Man who is capable of so infamous a Calling as that of a Spy, is not very much to be relied upon. He will be more industrious to carry that which is grateful, than that which is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting, narrating, or using informants as plot devices, account for bias and invention: spies and gossipers will amplify, aggravate, and pervert facts for favour or malice. Writers should check facts, avoid trusting single clandestine sources, and show how rumor inflates inferences (the 'Palace of Fame' / echo metaphor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete social scenes and anecdotes to expose manners
rubrics_metrics.description: Sempronia... knows all that passes in every Quarter... At the Price of a good Sum of Money, Sempronia... brought about the Match... To rob a Lady at Play of Half her Fortune, is not so ill, as giving the whole and her self to an unworthy Husband... The Infirmary anecdote: send the sulky, the dull, the peevish, the pun-hating, the noisy disputant to the Infirmary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrate abstract morals and social faults through vivid, specific episodes and character sketches. Small domestic scenes (dinners, matchmaking stratagems, clubs' eccentric rules) provide comedic and satirical leverage to reveal larger social norms and consequences; use concrete detail to make satire evident and memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame satire to show comparative harms and moral consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: To murder and to rob are less Iniquities, than to raise Profit by Abuses, as irreparable as taking away Life; but more grievous, as making it lastingly unhappy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire should not merely ridicule; it ought to show why a vice is especially harmful. Emphasize the long-term or systemic damage of certain social practices (e.g., marrying for money, profiteering by abuses) so the moral point is clear rather than merely mocking individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mean-spirited irony that 'picks on' the powerless
rubrics_metrics.description: The Snarler... exerts themselves most against these below them, you see their Humour best, in their Talk to their Servants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irony and sarcasm directed at those less powerful (servants, dependents) mark poor taste and petty humour. When deploying irony, direct it toward appropriate targets (hypocrisy, vice, affectation) rather than punching down; ensure satirical voice preserves moral authority rather than cruelty.
